items.note: NOT DOING THIS — the premise is wrong, and it is measured. AzerothCore has NO grid state machine in this version: the only caller of MapGridManager::UnloadGrid is Map::UnloadAll, which runs at shutdown. Instances are unloaded whole when they empty; continents keep every grid they ever touched, for the life of the process. So our behaviour already matches upstream. It is also not a leak but a BOUNDED WORKING SET: a map is 64x64 grids, and the largest content maps hold ~58k spawns (map 0: 29,678 creatures + 28,649 gameobjects; map 571: 33,519 + 14,441). MEASURED (GridResidencyTests): every terrain tile of Eastern Kingdoms resident is 687 tiles and 171 MB, about 255 KB per tile. Four fully-explored continents would be roughly 700 MB of terrain. Substantial, bounded, and the same shape upstream carries. Revisit only if memory becomes a real constraint — and if it does, unloading INSTANCES when they empty is upstream's answer and the one to copy, not per-grid unloading.

items.text: Health, powers and death state saved
items.note: The board note was stale: level, money and experience were ALREADY written with the position. What was missing is health, the seven powers, PLAYER_FLAGS and the corpse-reclaim penalty window. THE DEATH STATE IS THE ONE THAT MATTERED — a player who logged out dead came back ALIVE, which undoes the corpse, the reclaim penalty and the durability charge in a single loading screen and makes every death optional. Upstream derives the state from the ghost bit in PLAYER_FLAGS on load (PlayerStorage.cpp: HasPlayerFlag(GHOST) -> DeathState::Dead), and so does this. Restoring the flags WITHOUT the state leaves a character that IsGhost calls a ghost and IsAlive calls alive — a state nothing else knows how to be in, and one that lets a corpse swing a sword. All SEVEN powers, like upstream: a druid holds rage and energy at once, so saving only the class's 'current' resource loses the rest. Values are CLAMPED on restore because the maximum is recomputed from the base tables every login, and a character whose level or gear changed would otherwise come back over its own cap. A health of ZERO is read as 'never saved' rather than 'died', since the two are indistinguishable — that costs one corpse its state exactly once, on the first login after this. The penalty window is restored OUTSIDE that guard, so an unsaved character does not get a free reset. SaveProgressAsync now takes a CharacterProgress record: it had ten positional parameters and would have had eighteen, which is one transposition away from writing health into mana with nothing to catch it.

items.text: Swim/fly distinction
items.note: Swimming state is read and acted on — drowning, fatigue and lava all key off it. What is still not done is REFUSING a client that claims to swim where there is no water, and that is now purely a margin problem: a player who just jumped clear of a lake is legitimately dry at a position they send while still flagged swimming. Needs a tolerance in time and distance before it can reject anything.

items.text: Speed checks against applied speeds rather than a fixed ceiling
items.note: The validator is held to the player's own fastest forward speed times a tolerance of 2, instead of a flat 60 — four times tighter for a player at base run. The tolerance is deliberately loose because the elapsed time is the server's, so a stalled tick or a burst of queued packets inflates the measured speed; it has NOT been validated against a real client under latency. CMSG_FORCE_*_SPEED_CHANGE_ACK is now handled, which is what closes the ambiguity: while any ordered speed is unacknowledged the check falls back to the flat ceiling, because the client is legitimately at either the old value or the new one and the server cannot tell which. Only the LAST acknowledgement of a run is compared — several changes can be in flight and every earlier reply is stale on arrival. A mismatch re-sends the correct speed rather than kicking, which is a deliberate deviation from upstream for the same reason the rest of the validator corrects instead of disconnecting.

items.text: Drowning, fatigue and lava damage
items.note: Mirror timers: a breath bar under water, a fatigue bar in dark water, and a fire timer on contact with lava or slime. Each drains while its condition holds, refills ten times faster once it stops, and bills once a SECOND while empty rather than once a tick — the expiry adds a second back instead of resetting. Damage is returned to the map to apply, so death is still noticed in one place. Ghosts do not drown. Water Breathing disables the bar entirely while ModWaterBreathing multiplies its length — the two look interchangeable and are not. Gaining the first mid-drown clears a bar already running rather than freezing it part-drained.

items.text: Fall damage
items.note: FallDamage.Calculate is upstream's line — nothing under 13.48 yards hurts, then 1.8% of maximum health per yard, capped at maximum health and fatal around 70. Measured from the last height the SERVER saw the player supported at, not from the client's own FallTime or fall-start position, both of which are what a client dodging fall damage would understate. Landing in liquid costs nothing, checked against the liquid at the landing point rather than the swimming flag, which the client clears while jumping under water. Safe Fall and Slow Fall are wired now: Safe Fall takes yards off the measured drop and stacks, Slow Fall removes the damage outright — two different auras with two different behaviours, and reading either as the other is a rogue who never dies to a fall.

items.text: DotRecast — no fork needed
items.note: DECISION RESOLVED, and it turned out not to be a decision. The fear was that AzerothCore's patched Detour (DT_POLYREF64 plus a 12/21/31 salt/tile/poly split) made its tiles unreadable by a stock port. Only the reference WIDTH reaches the disk, through sizeof(dtLink), and all 400 sampled tiles measure as 64-bit — which DotRecast is too (DtLink.refs is a long). The PACKING never reaches the disk: DtNavMesh.AddTile takes a parsed DtMeshData with no link array, and Detour rebuilds every link itself, so a poly ref is created and consumed inside one process and never compared against anything AzerothCore wrote. Stock DotRecast.Detour from NuGet, no fork, no vendored third-party codebase.

items.text: Load a real tile into a mesh and run a path
items.note: Done: 515 tiles of Eastern Kingdoms load into a stock DtNavMesh, and FindPath runs between two points near the human start. The swizzle is (y, z, x) straight from PathGenerator — NOT negated. Negating it (which the terrain tiles' origin-centred inversion tempts you into) puts the point outside the mesh and comes back as "no polygon here" rather than as an error, which is what happened on the first attempt. Still to do: comparing our path against the C++ server's for the same endpoints, which needs a running C++ server.

items.text: PathGenerator and the (y, z, x) swizzle
items.note: Corners come from findStraightPath (the funnel algorithm — the optimal route in two dimensions), then each leg is walked along the surface in four-yard steps with each step's height taken from the polygon under it. Corners alone are not walkable: a leg between two of them is a straight line in THREE dimensions, so a long one cuts through a rise. Measured near the human start, sampled points sit within 1.4 yards of the terrain where a straight interpolation strays 3.7 — the test bound is 3, chosen to fail the second and pass the first rather than to be safe. Upstream's steering loop is not ported: it re-derives each corner as it goes and we already have them all from the funnel. Each sample is lifted 0.5 yards (upstream's result[1] += 0.5f) because the mesh sits below where feet rest. NavMeshManager loads tiles lazily around a point plus neighbours. THREE tile formats, TWO naming conventions: .map and .mmtile are {map}{gridX}{gridY}, .vmtile swaps them.

items.text: Custom cost function: dist × (1 + slopeDegrees/100) × areaCost, and DT_SLOPE_TOO_STEEP
items.note: Ported from dtQueryFilterExt::getCost: distance x (1 + slopeDegrees/100), so a route up a hillside costs more than the same distance across a field and a creature prefers to go round. Area costs are left at Detour's default of 1 — upstream never calls setAreaCost either, so the term is present in the formula and inert in both.

items.text: Creature movement follows a real route
items.note: Map.SendCreatureMove asks the navmesh for a route and walks its corners, one move per corner, because the client interpolates a leg at a time. A straight line remains the FALLBACK and has to: 98 maps of several hundred have a navmesh, any tile can be missing, and a creature that refused to move without a route would stand still everywhere else. Re-pathing compares the target against where the creature is ultimately heading, not against the next corner — comparing corners re-paths every tick on any route with a bend. A route survives having a victim: Update withholds the GENERATOR's next destination during a fight, and the remaining corners are not the generator's. Wander is routed too, through a RouteTo delegate the map hands the creature — the same arrangement as FloorAt, so Creature still knows nothing about maps. Worth it by measurement: 24,712 of 77,138 wandering spawns (32%) have a radius above the 5-yard pathing threshold; the other 68% are short hops that stay straight lines. A routed wander AMBLES — MoveAlong was written for chases and runs by default, and inheriting that would have every critter in the world moving as though alarmed.

phases.title: Combat
phases.summary: Melee is done end to end and verified by a headless gate. Spells cast, deal damage, and apply auras that tick on the map's clock.

items.text: RollMeleeOutcomeAgainst — one urand(0, 10000) against a running sum
items.note: In the order miss, dodge, parry, block, glancing, crushing, crit, normal. Reproduced structurally, including the (tmp -= skillBonus) > 0 mutation inside the branch conditions.

Facing asymmetry: only a player victim loses its dodge from behind
items.note: Parry and block are lost by anyone. That is what makes tanking a boss survivable, not an oversight.

items.text: creature_template.flags_extra vendored and wired — the five bits that gate table branches

Evading clears the threat list, not only the victim

CMSG_CAST_SPELL and its target block, whose layout is decided by a leading mask
items.note: Five separate flags share ONE guid field, not one each.

items.note: The first is whatever produced the cast, the second is always the unit; writing it once shifts every field after it by a guid.

items.text: THE GLOBAL COOLDOWN BLOCKS ONLY SPELLS THAT WOULD START ONE
items.note: An ability with no StartRecoveryTime — Heroic Strike, say — is usable during it.

POWER SLOTS ARE INDEXED BY TYPE
items.note: Power used to always read slot 0, so a warrior's rage went into the mana field — a full mana bar and an empty rage bar on the same unit.

items.text: A SINGLE DIE SIDE ADDS EXACTLY 1 AND DRAWS NO RANDOM NUMBER
items.note: Upstream has an explicit case 1; folding it into irand(1, 1) gives the same answer and desynchronises the stream.

items.text: SCHOOL_DAMAGE, HEAL, and the three weapon-damage forms — 4 of upstream's 164
A WEAPON-DAMAGE EFFECT'S VALUE IS A FLAT BONUS ON TOP OF A SWING
items.note: Treating it as damage makes Heroic Strike hit for 11 instead of a swing plus 11.

items.text: Armour is applied ONCE AT THE END, not per effect
items.note: It ceilings, so per-effect mitigation gains a point per effect.

items.text: SMSG_SPELLNONMELEEDAMAGELOG — THE TARGET IS WRITTEN BEFORE THE CASTER
items.note: The opposite order to SMSG_ATTACKERSTATEUPDATE, with nothing in either packet saying so.

items.text: 3.3.5a HAS NO AURA UPDATE FIELDS — the client learns about auras from SMSG_AURA_UPDATE alone, keyed by slot
items.note: Earlier clients carried them in the unit's field block, and every guide written for those still says so. Only UNIT_FIELD_AURASTATE survives here.

items.text: AuraEffect / Aura / AuraContainer — effects, duration, slots
items.note: Slots are lowest-free rather than a running counter: the client indexes a fixed 255-wide space, and a counter would run off the end of a long session.

items.text: THE FIRST TICK IS A FULL PERIOD AWAY, not immediate
items.note: A damage-over-time that ticks the instant it lands is a direct hit with extra steps, and it front-loads every such spell.

items.text: The tick loop is a WHILE and THE REMAINDER CARRIES FORWARD
items.note: An out-of-phase map hands in four ticks' worth of diff at once, so a tick longer than the amplitude is the normal case. Resetting the timer instead of adding to it stretches the period and loses ticks.

items.text: Expiry is checked AFTER ticking, so an aura's last tick lands
items.note: Checking first drops one tick from every damage-over-time in the game — an 8 s burn paying for four and landing three.

items.text: A recast from the same caster refreshes in place and KEEPS ITS SLOT; two casters each get their own
items.note: Keeping the slot stops the buff bar flickering the icon away and back on every refresh.

items.text: SMSG_AURA_UPDATE — the caster guid appears only when the CASTER flag is CLEAR, the two durations only when the DURATION flag is set
A removal is the slot and a ZERO SPELL ID, and the packet ends there
SMSG_PERIODICAURALOG, whose trailer differs per aura type
Ticks go through the same damage path as a swing: threat, death and experience all follow
items.note: A burn can kill something after its caster has walked away, and the caster is looked up rather than held because it may be gone.

items.text: Death clears every aura and tells the client about each one
Stacking, charges, dispel and proc triggers
MOD_STAT, MOD_INCREASE_SPEED and MOD_DECREASE_SPEED do something
items.note: Slows and speed buffs recompute the unit's speeds and go out on the wire — the controller gets SMSG_FORCE_*_SPEED_CHANGE with a counter it acknowledges, observers get SMSG_SPLINE_SET_* so their copy interpolates at the right rate. Only RUN carries an extra byte in the forced form, and leaving it out shifts the float. The rule that matters: speed modifiers take the STRONGEST (MaxPositive/MaxNegative) while stat modifiers SUM (Total) — that is per aura type upstream, not a convention, and picking one rule for both is wrong in one direction or the other. A buff and a slow compound (1.5 x 0.5 = 0.75) rather than cancelling. Recomputed from the unit's OWN base speeds, kept alongside the live ones, because a creature's template scales its walk and run at spawn. ModDamageDone is still unhandled.

items.text: player_xp_for_level vendored — 79 rows. EACH ROW IS THE COST OF LEAVING THAT LEVEL
items.note: Not a running total; reading it as a total makes every level after the first cost far too much.

items.text: Acore::XP::BaseGain — two different curves either side of the player's level
GetGrayLevel (three segments, flat floor under 6) and GetZeroDifference (a nine-step widening function)
items.note: Neither derivable from the other.

items.text: The base figure comes from the CONTENT, not the creature's level: 45 classic, 235 Outland, 580 Northrend
Elite pays double — and RARE IS NOT ELITE, despite ranking above world boss numerically
Critters and anything flagged NoExperience pay nothing
items.note: Or a field of rabbits is a levelling strategy.

items.text: GiveXP as a LOOP, with the surplus carried forward — one kill can cross several levels
Level-up recomputes health, mana and the five attributes, and REFILLS health and mana
SMSG_LOG_XPGAIN, whose LAYOUT DEPENDS ON WHETHER THERE WAS A VICTIM
SMSG_LEVELUP_INFO, which carries DELTAS RATHER THAN TOTALS, in fixed-size arrays
Experience is paid BEFORE the threat list is cleared
items.note: Creature.Kill forgets everyone, so paying afterwards pays nobody and looks like a kill that simply awards nothing.

items.text: tools/harness/m5_combat.py — an M5 gate driving the whole loop over the real protocol
items.note: Log in, walk to a wolf, auto-attack, kill it, gain experience. Measured: ~9 swings each way, 50 experience for a level 1 kill. Passes repeatedly.

items.text: A PLAYER HAD NO WEAPON DAMAGE AND NO ATTACK TIME
items.note: Both are update fields defaulting to zero, so an unequipped character swung every tick for nothing, with no error anywhere — M5 was literally unreachable. Found by writing the gate, not by any unit test.

items.text: Verify against a real 3.3.5a client
items.note: The gate proves the server's packets are self-consistent and carry the right numbers; it cannot prove the client reads them the same way. Only a real client can answer that.

phases.title: Progression systems
phases.summary: Inventory, loot, quests, vendors, trainers, gossip, talents, reputation, corpses, chat, commands. Death, items, bags, loot, quests, gossip and vendors are done. Trainers need a spellbook, which does not exist yet.

items.text: Player death lands on Corpse, the same promotion a creature makes — JustDied is the moment things that happen once happen, not a state anything updates in
THE THREE STATES ARE NOT TWO: alive, a corpse that cannot move, and a ghost that can
items.note: The client keys movement off the health value, so a ghost gets 1 point and not 0. Leave it at zero after release and the player is stuck on the spot with the release button gone.

items.text: A creature that kills a player forgets it and goes home
items.note: Without this it stands over the corpse swinging at something the swing loop refuses to hit, forever — the player never releases, so nothing ever clears the threat list.

items.text: The corpse position is remembered at release, which is what a corpse run walks back to
CMSG_REPOP_REQUEST releases to the nearest usable graveyard; CMSG_RECLAIM_CORPSE resurrects at the body
Resurrecting restores half health and mana, and EMPTIES RAGE rather than halving it
items.note: Rage is earned in combat. Half a bar you did not fight for is a different resource.

items.text: game_graveyard_zone vendored (700 links across 163 zones); coordinates come from WorldSafeLocs.dbc
items.note: Newer AzerothCore reads them from a game_graveyard table the vendored dump predates. The same divergence as creature_template_model — the data is what this follows. Measured: a human dying at the Northshire start releases 58 yards away, to 'Elwynn Forest, Northshire'.

items.text: The faction filter runs before the distance comparison
items.note: 570 of the 700 rows are neutral, so forgetting it looks like it works — until a contested zone leaves a player with nowhere to go.

items.text: A graveyard on another map is skipped, and a zone with none leaves the ghost where it fell
items.note: There is no cross-map transfer yet. Releasing somewhere unreachable is worse than not moving; standing over your own corpse, you can still reclaim.

items.text: Resurrection sickness, and the spirit healer's own resurrect
items.note: This is what makes the two ways back from death DIFFERENT, and without it the corpse run has no reason to exist. Walking to your corpse is free and slow; the spirit healer is instant and charges twice: a QUARTER of your durability including the BAGS (dying itself takes a tenth off equipment only — same method, different arguments, and the difference is the whole design), plus resurrection sickness. The sickness is spell 15007 in three bands, not one. Below level 11 there is none at all — a character in their starting zone dies constantly and ten minutes of halved stats there is most of a play session. From 11 it is a minute per level above ten, reaching the full ten minutes at 20. THE DURATION IS OVERRIDDEN rather than taken from the spell: 15007 carries the full ten minutes, so casting it and leaving the duration alone gives a level-11 character the same sentence as a level-80 raider. Tested against a real client at two levels, which is the only way to catch that. No corpse-range check, unlike reclaiming — working wherever the ghost stands is the point. The NPC flag is checked server-side: the guid arrives from the client, and without it any creature in the world would resurrect you from anywhere.

items.text: A real Corpse object, visible to everyone
items.note: Was a remembered position on the player — enough to walk back to and reclaim, and invisible to everyone including its owner. The client draws the body from a real object and offers the resurrect dialog because one is nearby. CREATED AT RELEASE, NOT AT DEATH: until a player releases, the body standing there IS their own character, still rendered dead. Creating it at death puts two of them in the world. THE APPEARANCE IS REPACKED, NOT COPIED. A player keeps skin/face/hair-style/hair-colour in PLAYER_BYTES and facial hair in PLAYER_BYTES_2; a corpse wants race and gender in its first word alongside skin and the rest in the second. Copying the player's words across gives a body with somebody else's face — which looks like a plausible character, not like a bug. Equipment slots hold a DISPLAY ID plus inventory type packed into one word, not an item guid or entry. The create block is NOT UpdateFlag.Living — a corpse does not move, so it carries a stationary position like a gameobject (LOWGUID | STATIONARY_POSITION | POSITION, minus the rotation). Sending the living form makes the client read a movement block, speeds and fall time out of bytes that are not there. It uses the Corpse field-visibility table, which already existed unused. Reclaiming, the spirit healer and dying again all convert the old body to BONES rather than deleting it, so clients already told about it see it change instead of vanishing — then it is removed, since nothing decays bones yet. LIMITS: corpses are not persisted, so they vanish on restart (upstream saves them to a table). Player.CorpsePosition remains the authority for the reclaim range check; the object is what is rendered. The two are parallel rather than unified.

items.text: The corpse reclaim delay, now enforced
items.note: Was sent and never enforced — the worst of both, since the client counted down a timer the server ignored, so an honest player waited and anyone clicking through did not. SEPARATE BUG FOUND AND FIXED at the same site: SMSG_CORPSE_RECLAIM_DELAY was being sent the six-minute RELEASE timer instead of the reclaim delay, so the client showed a six-minute wait. Two different numbers for two different things. THE LADDER IS NOT 1st/2nd/3rd DEATH. copseReclaimDelay is {30, 60, 120}, but UpdateCorpseReclaimDelay sets the window to one step BEYOND however many are left — so a second death with the whole first window still open lands on the THIRD rung (120), not the second. The middle rung is reachable only by dying again LATE in the window, when most of it has decayed (traced: second death 250s in gives 60). Writing the obvious 30/60/120 ladder halves the penalty for chain-dying and looks completely right. The penalty is a 5-minute WINDOW rather than a death counter, which is what lets it fade with no 'reset the count' call to forget. The wait runs from the DEATH, not the release — a player reading the release dialog has already served it. The delay is fixed at death rather than recomputed on reclaim, or a long corpse run would shorten its own penalty as the window decayed underneath it.

items.text: item_template vendored — 38,610 rows, 150 columns
items.note: sql/world/ grows from ~28 MB to ~42 MB. The vendoring rule says a fresh clone must be able to start, and that is the price.

items.text: THE STORE IS WIDE WHERE THE OTHERS ARE NARROW, and has to be
items.note: Nearly every column is written straight back out in the query response — that packet is how the client draws a tooltip it has never seen. Reading a subset means an item missing whatever was left out.

items.text: GetMaxStackSize — zero, negative and int.MaxValue all mean 0x7FFFFFFE
items.note: Read literally, a stackable of 0 is an item nobody can hold and the -1 the table uses for coins is a stack of four billion.

items.text: Item is an Object but NOT a WorldObject — 64 field slots against a unit's 148
items.note: No position, no map, no movement block. It reaches a client because that client owns it, not because it is nearby.

items.text: A container is a Bag, whose block runs 74 slots further to CONTAINER_END
items.note: The client reads the extra slots the moment the container type bit is set. Verified: all 155 bags in the table fit the client's 36-slot array.

items.text: A fresh item holds ONE, not a full stack; durability starts full; spell charges keep their sign
items.note: A negative charge count is what destroys the item at zero — store the absolute value and an empty potion stays in the bag forever.

items.text: SMSG_ITEM_QUERY_SINGLE_RESPONSE — nearly every field is FOUR BYTES regardless of its column
items.note: class is a tinyint in the table and a uint32 on the wire, because the C++ struct widens it on load.

items.text: The stat count is a length prefix; the three unused name slots are ONE ZERO BYTE each
items.note: Writing all ten stats regardless, or three words for the names, shifts the whole tail.

items.text: A spell slot is six words whether or not the spell exists, and -1 cooldowns mean ASK THE SPELL
items.note: Sending the -1 through shows a clickable item with a four-billion-millisecond cooldown. Needed Spell.dbc's Category column, which was not being read.

items.text: A missing item answers with the entry and the high bit set, not with silence
items.note: A zeroed body instead leaves the client believing in a nameless item, which it caches to disk and stops asking about.

items.text: All 38,610 rows write as a query response without throwing; longest is 699 bytes
Random properties, enchantments and gems
Item duration ticking down, and the item disappearing when it runs out
locales_item — every tooltip is English
150 slots in ONE FLAT GUID ARRAY, whatever the five field names suggest
items.note: INV_SLOT_HEAD, PACK_SLOT_1, BANK_SLOT_1 and the rest are consecutive names for consecutive stretches of the same run. Adding a range's own base to a range-relative slot puts the backpack 46 words too far along.

items.text: THE BACKPACK IS CONTAINER 255, NOT 0
items.note: Bag 0 is a real bag in the first bag slot. Reading a bag byte of zero as the backpack sends every query to whatever is worn there — and finds nothing, because it is usually empty.

items.text: A packed position puts the BAG IN THE HIGH BYTE, and three of the six opcodes read the DESTINATION FIRST
items.note: Reading them the intuitive way round swaps the drag: the item the player picked up stays put and the one under the cursor moves.

items.text: FindEquipSlot — inventory type to slot, with two candidates for rings, trinkets and one-handers
AN EMPTY OFF HAND IS NOT A FREE ONE when a two-hander is worn
items.note: Checking only whether the slot holds something says it is free, and the player ends up with a greatsword and a shield. Equipping a two-hander displaces the off-hand item, and is refused outright if there is nowhere for it to go.

items.text: Nobody can dual wield, because it is SPELL 674 and there is no spellbook
items.note: Correct at level 1 and wrong from level 10. A class trait would be the easy wrong answer.

items.text: Storing fills partial stacks before taking a free slot, and places NOTHING if it cannot fit everything
items.note: Half a loot drop landing and the rest vanishing is worse than none of it landing — the player has no way to know what they lost.

items.text: Split, swap, destroy — and a NON-EMPTY BAG can be neither destroyed nor swapped out
items.note: Its contents have their own guids. Destroying the bag strands them: still owned, in no slot, written back out as rows pointing at a bag that no longer exists.

items.text: CharStartOutfit.dbc is where starting gear lives — NOT playercreateinfo_item
items.note: The vendored world table has a single row in the whole database. Reading only it produces a naked character with no error anywhere. Race, class and gender are single BYTES in the DBC; reading them as words makes every row an outfit for race 0.

items.text: item_instance and character_inventory, saved whole rather than diffed
items.note: An item can move, stack, split and vanish within one tick. Reconciling that would duplicate the inventory's own bookkeeping, and a stale row is the failure that duplicates items.

items.text: Item guids are allocated IN MEMORY and seeded from MAX(guid) at startup
items.note: The client is told an item's guid before any row exists, so the column cannot be auto-increment. Reissuing one makes two items share an identity and one overwrites the other on the next save.

items.text: A bag is stored by its OWN GUID, not the slot it is worn in
items.note: Moving a bag between bag slots would otherwise mean rewriting every row inside it.

items.text: Items ride in the player's own create packet at login, and get values blocks after
items.note: A slot guid pointing at an object the client has never been told about draws an empty square. Nothing pushed changed fields to the client at all before this — health, experience and level were all silently server-side.

items.text: SMSG_INVENTORY_CHANGE_FAILURE — a code of zero is the WHOLE PACKET, and the two guids are FULL not packed
The character list draws what each character owns
EQUIPPING A WEAPON CHANGES THE SWING — damage, speed, armour and the five attributes
items.note: Without it the sword is drawn, the tooltip is right, and the damage never changes. Attack power is scaled by the weapon's OWN speed; a fixed 2000 ms makes a slow weapon and a fast one hit the same. Verified through the M5 gate: the starting sword took the kill from 8 swings to 5.

items.text: Stats are recomputed from the level's base each time, never adjusted by a delta
items.note: A delta is one missed call away from a character who gains strength every time they take a belt off, and nothing would ever notice.

items.text: A BROKEN item gives nothing — no damage, no stats, no armour
The bank, bought bank bag slots and the keyring
items.note: Buyback landed with the vendor work; the bank, bank bag purchases and the keyring are now in. The slots ALWAYS existed in the flat 150-slot array — nothing could reach them — so persistence covered them the moment something could put an item there. The stacking planner was GENERALISED over a position sequence rather than copied: CanStore and CanBank are the same routine over different slots, and a second copy drifts the first time one learns something the other does not. TWO TRAPS, both caught by tests. (1) The item being moved must be EXCLUDED from its own limit check, or banking your one unique trinket is refused because you already have one — which is true, and is the item in your hand. (2) The slot being VACATED counts as free, or a move within the same region cannot pick the slot the item is already in, and something banked twice walks along the bank one slot at a time. That surfaced as a failing no-op test, not by inspection. The item leaves its slot only AFTER somewhere is found for it — the obvious order (pick up, then put down) loses the item when the destination is full. Bank bags are usable only in slots PAID FOR: the client draws exactly as many as PLAYER_BYTES_2 byte 2 says, and the slot in the packet comes from the client. BANK SLOT PRICES DIVERGE FROM UPSTREAM, deliberately. BankBagSlotPrices.dbc has TWELVE rows but only SEVEN bag slots exist; rows 8-12 carry a sentinel price of 999,999,999 copper. Upstream will sell an eighth slot to anyone who can pay — the client's money ceiling is above that — and the slot then does not exist. We refuse past seven. A gated test pins the shape of that data. Also note SMSG_BUY_BANK_SLOT_RESULT reads FAILURE-FIRST: Ok is 3, not 0, so a zero-means-success habit reports every purchase as 'you cannot have any more'. KEYRING: items with BAG_FAMILY_MASK_KEYS (156 of them in the content) try the 32 keyring slots first and OVERFLOW into ordinary bag space when it is full, rather than being refused. STILL OPEN: bag families for ordinary bags (quiver, herb bag, etc.).

items.text: Soulbinding, unique constraints and item limit categories
items.note: Done, along with weapon/armour proficiency earlier. BINDING happens in Place, not in the equip path — everything that puts an item anywhere (loot, purchase, a GM command) goes through Place, and binding only on equip would leave a bind-on-pickup item tradeable for as long as it sat in a bag. Bind-on-pickup and quest items bind wherever they land; BIND-ON-EQUIP BINDS ONLY WHEN WORN, and that half is load-bearing: a BoE item is worth something on the market right up until somebody wears it, and binding it on pickup is a one-word change that quietly destroys the gear economy. The flag lives on ITEM_FIELD_FLAGS where the CLIENT reads it — tracking it server-side only leaves the tooltip saying 'tradeable', which is worse than not binding at all because it invites a trade that then fails. IsBoundToSomeoneElse is three cases and only one refuses: unbound is never someone else's and bound-to-you is not either; collapsing to 'is it bound' makes your own gear unequippable. TWO SEPARATE CAPS that read identically in prose. MaxCount and a 'have' category limit what is CARRIED; the unique-equipped flag and an 'equip' category limit what is WORN. A MaxCount of 0, -1 or int.MaxValue all mean no limit — most items leave the column at zero, so reading it literally makes almost everything in the game impossible to pick up. The limit CATEGORY exists because the cap is shared across different items: capping each mana gem separately lets you carry one of each, which is exactly what 'one mana gem' prevents. The mode column decides which cap it is, and an 'equip' category must NOT refuse a pick-up or a player cannot loot a second trinket they may own. The equip check excludes the slot being filled, or swapping a unique ring for the same ring refuses because the one coming off is still counted. An unknown category refuses rather than passes, since passing turns a data gap into an unlimited item. New DBC: ItemLimitCategory (83 rows), injected into Inventory rather than looked up globally so tests need no client.

items.text: Item ratings and resistances — only the five attributes are applied
Agility's contribution to armour, which needs the gt* DBCs
Other players see equipment, health and level change
items.note: Values blocks are broadcast to every observer who has the object, filtered per observer by UpdateFieldVisibilityRules. Map.BroadcastFieldChanges runs after everything that can dirty a field and before the flush, because the flush is where a player builds its own unfiltered block and clears its own mask. Create blocks are filtered the same way now, which closed a leak: a stranger walking past was being sent the whole non-zero field set, coinage included.

items.text: creature_loot_template (336,755 rows) and reference_loot_template (14,188) vendored
MINCOUNTORREF IS A COUNT WHEN POSITIVE AND A REFERENCE ID WHEN NEGATIVE
items.note: Read as a count regardless, every shared drop list becomes a request for a negative number of items — which, unsigned, is four billion.

items.text: A NEGATIVE CHANCE IS A QUEST DROP, and the chance is its absolute value
items.note: There is no separate flag. Reading the sign as part of the chance makes every quest item in the game impossible.

items.text: lootid is NOT the creature entry
items.note: Usually the same, often not — several entries share one list, and zero means it drops nothing at all.

items.text: A GROUP MEMBER WITH A CHANCE OF ZERO IS EQUAL-CHANCED, NOT IMPOSSIBLE
items.note: Most groups in the table are entirely zero-chance members. Treating zero as 0% means those groups never drop anything.

items.text: A group's explicit chances share ONE roll, subtracting as it walks
items.note: Rolling each member separately lets one group drop two items, which is the one thing a group exists to prevent.

items.text: maxcount on a REFERENCE row is how many rolls, not a stack size
A stack larger than the item allows is split across slots
items.note: A loot slot holds one stack. Handing over 30 linen in one slot makes an illegal stack the moment it is picked up.

items.text: The money roll's third branch: a range wider than 32,700 is rolled in units of 256
items.note: Nothing in a starting zone reaches it, which is why it is easy to drop and never notice. The answer is always a multiple of 256.

items.text: UNIT_DYNFLAG_LOOTABLE is what makes a corpse sparkle — without it the client never sends CMSG_LOOT
items.note: An empty pile is deliberately NOT flagged: a sparkling corpse that opens an empty window is worse than one that does not sparkle.

items.text: SMSG_LOOT_RESPONSE — the count is of the SLOTS WRITTEN, not the pile's size
items.note: A taken slot is left out and keeps its number, so the count and the highest number disagree. The client sends the number back, so renumbering makes the next click land on the wrong item.

items.text: A refusal is the same opcode with a loot type of zero
items.note: The client has already drawn the window frame; silence leaves it up, empty and unclosable.

items.text: CMSG_AUTOSTORE_LOOT_ITEM carries a slot and NO GUID — the server remembers which window is open
THE SLOT IS MARKED TAKEN ONLY AFTER THE ITEM IS STORED
items.note: Marking first loses the item when the bags are full: gone from the window and nothing holding it.

items.text: Money goes in the purse and the window is cleared with two packets, not one
items.note: SMSG_LOOT_CLEAR_MONEY empties the coin line; the notify is only the chat message. Sending the notify alone leaves the coins drawn.

items.text: Rolled every loot template under 3,000 and every reference resolves
items.note: Verified live through the M5 gate: a Diseased Young Wolf dropped a Diseased Wolf Pelt, which went into the bags.

Quest drops are flagged and shown to everyone
items.note: Nobody has any quests, so filtering them would hide every one of them.

items.note: MEASURED, and it is not the cheap win it looks like: 38,481 of the 38,594 spawned chests are LOCKED (gameobject_template.data0), so opening them without a lock system would be wrong for 99.7% of them — herb nodes gatherable without herbalism, locked chests opened without a key. Locks need Lock.dbc, and most of its entries are skill requirements, so this is gated on skills like proficiency is. The 113 unlocked spawns and the key-locked ones would work; the rest should refuse.

items.text: quest_template (9,464 rows, 70 columns read), creature_queststarter and creature_questender vendored
STARTER AND ENDER ARE SEPARATE TABLES, and very often different NPCs
items.note: Treating either as both puts the hand-in question mark over the wrong person. The M6 gate takes a quest from Deputy Willem and hands it to Eagan Peltskinner 86 yards away, precisely because a server that conflates them passes every unit test.

items.text: A NEGATIVE OBJECTIVE ENTRY IS A GAMEOBJECT, and the client wants id | 0x80000000
items.note: No column says which kind it is; the sign is the whole distinction. Sending -id leaves the client looking for a creature that does not exist and the objective line never moves.

items.text: RewardOrRequiredMoney is a REWARD when positive and a COST when negative
items.note: Read unsigned, a quest that costs gold pays out four billion copper.

items.text: QUESTXP.DBC IS INDEXED BY THE QUEST'S LEVEL, and RewardXPId is a COLUMN in that row
items.note: Looking the quest up by its own id finds nothing and every quest pays zero. A level of -1 means the player's level; read unsigned it becomes 65,535 and pays nothing.

items.text: The payout is rounded to a band — 5 below 100, then 10, then 25, then 50
items.note: Skipping it pays amounts the real client never shows: close enough to look right, and wrong in a way nothing flags.

items.text: Level 255 is a SENTINEL with no DBC row — four quests carry it and pay nothing
items.note: Upstream returns zero for a missing row too. The data being explicit, not a hole.

items.text: FOUR OBJECTIVE COUNTERS SHARE TWO UPDATE FIELDS, sixteen bits each
items.note: The pair is one 64-bit value to the client. A counter per field puts objective 0's count where the client reads all four.

items.text: A quest with NO objectives is complete the moment it is taken
items.note: A 'go and speak to someone' quest. Marking it incomplete leaves it uncompletable — nothing could ever finish it.

items.text: A kill credits EVERY quest that wants it, not the first
items.note: Two quests asking for the same creature is common, and crediting one is a bug a player notices and cannot explain.

items.text: ITEM OBJECTIVES ARE RECOUNTED FROM THE BAGS, never incremented
items.note: An item can arrive by looting, trading, buying or mail. An increment at each is four chances to miss one; a recount cannot drift. It is also why item counts are not persisted.

items.text: The record survives being handed in, which is what stops the quest being offered twice
items.note: Dropping it lets a player repeat every quest in the game by talking to the same NPC twice.

items.text: Class and race masks are bit masks over ONE-BASED ids, and zero means everyone
SMSG_QUESTGIVER_QUEST_DETAILS, _REQUEST_ITEMS, _OFFER_REWARD and _QUEST_COMPLETE
items.note: The details packet always writes four emote pairs; the offer packet writes only the used ones. Genuinely different shapes for the same idea.

items.text: A quest with no item objectives SKIPS the request-items window
items.note: It would have nothing to show and the player would be looking at an empty dialog.

items.text: The reward is paid in ONE place, and nothing is given if not everything fits
items.note: Splitting the payment across the complete and choose handlers is how a quest pays twice. A half-paid quest is worse than an unpaid one: it is gone from the log and the rest is unreachable.

items.text: The accept handler checks the NPC actually offers the quest
items.note: Without it a client can accept any quest in the game by naming its id at any NPC — the packet carries both.

items.text: character_queststatus, with the log slot and the four kill counters
tools/harness/m6_quest.py — the whole loop over the real protocol against real content

items.text: Quest chains — PrevQuestId, NextQuestId and exclusive groups
items.note: A quest's prerequisites are its own PrevQuestId PLUS every quest whose NextQuestId points back at it — the link is stored from either end, and 587 quests use the reverse direction, so reading only the forward column left all their successors ungated. Any ONE prerequisite satisfied is enough (they are alternatives, which is how two lines both open the same follow-up), except where the prerequisite sits in a NEGATIVE exclusive group, which is upstream's "each from all" and needs the whole group done. A POSITIVE group is "one from all": taking any locks out the rest (644 quests). Note upstream's own comment above SatisfyQuestExclusiveGroup describes the positive case backwards; the code beneath it is what the game does. Reputation, skill and timed quests are still absent and still pass.

Reputation and skill requirements, spell and title rewards, daily resets
gameobject_queststarter / _questender
items.note: Both vendored (447 starters, 457 enders). The whole quest conversation now resolves its giver to a small QuestGiver record covering creatures and objects alike, so accepting, handing in and the status marks all work from either. Creature and gameobject entries are SEPARATE keyspaces — entry 1234 is a different thing in each — so the two pairs of relation tables are kept apart. Reaching an object needs CMSG_GAMEOBJ_USE, which was not handled at all: the client sends questgiver-hello only for NPCs. Verified against the data: all 377 distinct starter entries are gameobject type 2 (questgiver), so the type gate excludes nothing, and 393 of them are spawned.

items.note: Found against a real client, which no gate could have caught. The details window is enough to accept a quest; the LOG entry needs the structured objectives, and the client will not draw a row for a quest whose data it has no copy of. Its reward arrays are written in FULL — there is no count in front of them, unlike every other quest packet.

items.note: The third time the two reference trees have diverged on a column name, after creature_template_model and game_graveyard.

GOSSIP LINES ARE FILTERED BY THE NPC'S OWN FLAG, which is the whole mechanism
items.note: One row saying 'I want to browse your goods' — menu 0, option 1 — serves every vendor in the game, and appears only on an NPC with the vendor bit. Ignoring the mask offers stabling and flight paths from a shopkeeper.

items.text: A NEGATIVE item IN NPC_VENDOR IS A REFERENCE to another vendor's whole list
items.note: The fourth table to overload a column's sign. Here it is caught loudly — the column is a signed mediumint, so an unsigned read throws — which is the lucky case. The loot table's version fails silently.

items.text: The quests ride in the SAME packet as the gossip lines
items.note: Which is what puts both in one window. Sending them separately produces two, and the client closes one at once.

items.text: SMSG_NPC_TEXT_UPDATE ALWAYS WRITES EIGHT BLOCKS
items.note: The client reads a fixed eight probability-and-text groups and picks between them. Writing only the one with something in it leaves it reading the rest of the packet as text.

items.text: VENDOR SLOTS ARE ONE-BASED, and unlimited stock is -1 rather than 0
items.note: The client subtracts one before sending a purchase back, so a zero-based slot buys the item before the one clicked. And a stock of zero greys the line out as sold.

items.text: An empty vendor list is a DIFFERENT SHAPE — a zero count and an error byte
items.note: Writing the ordinary form leaves the client waiting for a byte that never comes.

items.text: SMSG_BUY_FAILED's parameter word appears ONLY when it is non-zero
items.note: The packet's length is how the client tells whether one is there. A zero shifts the reason byte into it, and every failure reads as 'can't find item'.

items.text: The purchase count is a number of STACKS of BuyCount, not of items
items.note: Verified live: ten copper buys 200 Rough Arrows, because the row's BuyCount is 200.

items.text: An NPC with no gossip menu of its own goes STRAIGHT to what it does
items.note: A pure vendor opens its stock; a pure questgiver its quest. An empty gossip window first is a click the player should not have to make.

items.text: Selling: zero means the whole stack, a non-empty bag is refused, a success sends NOTHING
items.note: The item leaving the bag and the money arriving are both field updates; the client works the rest out.

items.text: tools/harness/m6_vendor.py — the whole shopping loop over the real protocol
items.note: It reads its own item guids out of the login update packet the way a real client does, which also proved the update-block encoding parses back correctly.

items.text: Flight masters, bankers, innkeepers, auctioneers and stable masters
items.note: Same shape as trainers: the line appears and clicking it closes the window.

items.text: Vendor stock limits and restock timers
items.note: maxcount and incrtime were being loaded and ignored — this is the runtime half. Stock is per VENDOR, not per entry: two innkeepers of the same template have their own shelves. maxcount counts ITEMS, not purchases, so a client buying one stack of twenty is asking for twenty of them — upstream uses BuyCount * count for both the check and the decrement. Restocking is lazy (nothing needs to know until somebody looks), happens on whole intervals only, and adds a purchase's worth per interval rather than one item. An incrtime of 0 means never refills. The ledger is sparse: unlimited rows never enter it and a fully restocked item is dropped from it. Stock is taken only after the sale goes through, so a purchase refused for bag space does not cost the vendor anything.

items.text: Extended cost — honour, arena points and tokens. Those lines are shown and refused.
The reputation discount on repair and vendor prices
items.note: Repair is done, and durability now actually moves: dying takes ten percent off what is WORN and nothing off what is carried (upstream passes inventory: false there — the spirit healer's twenty-five percent is a separate charge that does reach the bags). The loss always removes at least one point, because ten percent of a nine-durability item rounds to zero and those items would otherwise never wear out — which is most of what a level-one character is wearing. The bill multiplies points lost by a DurabilityCosts multiplier chosen by item LEVEL and kind, then by a DurabilityQuality modifier read at row (quality + 1) * 2 — not at the quality, which finds a row that exists and is wrong. Armour indexes twenty-one slots along from a weapon's, or a plate chestpiece is priced as a dagger. A zero bill is charged as one copper, upstream's own fix for artifact quality. CMSG_REPAIR_ITEM with an empty item guid means repair everything: the client sends the same opcode for both buttons. Repair-all goes item by item and stops when the money runs out, so a player short of the full amount still gets their weapon back. Inventory.Carried was added for the two 'and everything carried' passes — Inventory.All includes the equipment slots, which would wear a worn item twice per death. What is left here is the reputation discount, which needs a reputation system that does not exist.

items.text: The conditions system, which is how upstream picks between a menu's several texts
playercreateinfo_spell, playercreateinfo_spell_custom and npc_trainer vendored
THE STARTING SPELLS ARE IN playercreateinfo_spell, NOT THE _custom TABLE
items.note: The current C++ reads _custom, and in our dump that table is empty — the 182 real rows are in the older one. Fourth divergence between the two checkouts. Both are read, so either dump works.

items.text: Race and class masks are bits over ONE-BASED ids, and zero means everyone
items.note: Most of the table is zero-masked — the rows every character shares. Testing the bit without that shortcut leaves every character knowing nothing at all.

items.text: DUAL WIELD IS SPELL 674, NOT A CLASS TRAIT
items.note: Rogues and death knights start with it, a warrior learns it at level 20. Making it a trait gives every level-1 warrior an off-hand. Before the spellbook the off-hand slot was refused for everybody.

items.text: It is recomputed from the book, never toggled on learn
items.note: A toggle is one missed call away from a character who can dual wield because they once could.

items.text: SMSG_INITIAL_SPELLS — the count is SIXTEEN bits, and the cooldown count is not optional
items.note: The client builds its spellbook and action bars from this and nothing else. Verified live: a human warrior logs in knowing 51 spells.

items.text: The starting list is re-applied on EVERY login, not only at creation
items.note: The list grows. A character made before a spell was added would otherwise never get it, and learning is idempotent so it costs nothing.

items.text: CMSG_CAST_SPELL now refuses a spell the character has not learned
items.note: Until the spellbook existed it was honoured for any id in Spell.dbc — which is every spell in the game, from level one.

items.text: npc_trainer: a NEGATIVE SpellID is a reference to another trainer's whole list
items.note: The fifth table to overload a column's sign.

items.text: SMSG_TRAINER_LIST — each line carries two fixed arrays the client reads unconditionally
items.note: Two words of point cost and three of prerequisite spells. Both are zero and both must still be written, or the next line is read twenty bytes early.

items.text: The trainer gossip line opens something, and the list is resent after a purchase
items.note: So the line goes red rather than staying green until the window is reopened.

items.text: character_spell, saved whole like the inventory and the quest log
Spell ranks — a higher rank supersedes a lower one
items.note: SUPERSEDED, NOT REMOVED. Upstream keeps every rank in the book and flips the lower one INACTIVE, then sends SMSG_SUPERCEDED_SPELL(old, new) so the client swaps the action bar. Removing the old rank instead loses the fact the character ever had it, which matters the moment an unlearn or spec change has to put it back — and leaving the bar alone means the old rank stays exactly where the player's finger already is, so they keep casting it. THE RULE RUNS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS and the second is easy to miss: learning a LOWER rank than one already known must deactivate the NEW spell, not the old. That happens whenever a trainer's list is worked through out of order, and getting it backwards silently downgrades the character — they keep what they paid for and lose what they had. Superseding needs SAME CHAIN AND higher rank. Comparing ranks alone makes Fireball rank 3 supersede Frostbolt rank 2, since both are simply 'a rank'. Restore settles the ranks AFTER the whole set is in, because the database returns rows in no useful order — settling each as it lands deactivates a high rank that happened to be read before its own lower ones, and the character logs in having quietly lost their best spell. Chains come from spell_ranks (3,502 rows, 598 chains), newly vendored — nothing in the CLIENT's data says rank 3 supersedes rank 2, which is why upstream curates a table.

items.text: Skills — the block, the tables, and the trainer requirements that read them
items.note: Done. Skills live entirely in update fields — 127 slots of three words at PLAYER_SKILL_INFO_1_1, no packet at all — so writing them correctly IS making the skill window appear. The bonus word is packed the opposite way round from the two above it: temporary in the LOW half, permanent in the HIGH one (SKILL_TEMP_BONUS is PAIR32_LOPART). A slot's position is not the skill id — skills take the first free slot in the order learned and nothing sorts them, which is why the slot is remembered rather than computed and why it is not worth saving. NOTHING GRANTS A SKILL DIRECTLY: no table lists a warrior's starting skills. They arrive through SkillLineAbility rows whose AcquireMethod is 2, as a side effect of learning a spell — verified against a real client, a level-1 human warrior derives exactly 18 skills from playercreateinfo_spell (every weapon skill 1/5, the armour proficiencies 1/1, Common 300/300, Arms 5/5). How a bar is scaled is not a column anywhere: it comes from the category plus whether the skill has a tier row, and the check ORDER is the whole of it — a tier row wins over the category, then Runeforging is named outright against its own category (it is SKILL_CATEGORY_CLASS, which would otherwise give it a level bar), then armour is mono and languages are flat 300. Level-up raises the ceiling only, and leaves a maximum of 1 alone — that is how the grey bars are recognised without re-deriving the range. Death knights start level-scaled skills at (level-1)*5, not 1, or their starting zone is unplayable at 55. Trainer skill requirements are now enforced, and the check is TWO conditions: the skill must be present AND its value must meet the rank. A rank check alone passes trivially, since a missing skill reads as zero — and most rows have a rank of zero, so that mistake would leave the feature barely working. Player weapon/defence skill now reads the real value, falling back to level*5 when the skill is absent rather than to zero. Persisted in character_skills (value, max and step only — not the slot, not the bonuses). SKILL GAIN THROUGH USE is now in, for combat: the chance is 3 × lvldif × skillDiff / level, where the mob's level is capped at yours + 5 and the level difference is FLOORED AT 3 — without the floor a skill one point short of its cap can never be finished off against anything grey, and without the cap one exchange with a raid boss is worth a level's grinding. Intellect adds 2% per point but only on the ATTACKING side, which looks like a bug until you find it in the source. The chance is floored at 1%. Which outcomes teach is upstream's proc mask: hit, miss, dodge and parry teach; crit and glancing do not; a block teaches the DEFENDER only. Empty-handed raises Unarmed and Fist Weapons together and a fist weapon raises Unarmed too, so the two never drift; a fishing pole raises nothing (without that exception, beating something to death with one raises Fishing, since ForItem maps its subclass there). Gains are skipped entirely against players, or two characters could cap each other for free in a city.

items.text: playercreateinfo_action vendored, and SMSG_ACTION_BUTTONS at login
items.note: Without it the bars start empty and every spell has to be dragged out of the spellbook by hand — which works, and looks broken. Verified live: a level-1 human warrior logs in with 7 buttons.

items.text: ALL 144 BUTTONS ARE WRITTEN, empty ones included
items.note: There is no count and no index; the client reads them positionally, so a short packet fills the tail of the bars with whatever came next.

items.text: The action is the low 24 bits and the type the top byte of one word
items.note: Sent as separate fields, or with the type in the wrong byte, the client decodes an unknown type and draws the button as empty.

items.text: A packed action of ZERO clears the button — there is no separate opcode
The starting layout is applied only when nothing is saved
items.note: Unlike the starting spells, which are re-applied every login. A player who deliberately cleared a button would otherwise find it back.

items.text: Talents, specs and glyphs
Vendors, trainers, gossip
Talents and glyphs
Reputation
Basic chat — say, yell, whisper, emote
items.note: Say, yell, emote, text emote and whisper. THE SERVER DOES NOT GARBLE ANYTHING — it sends the real text plus the language id, and the client substitutes syllables for a language the listener has not learned. So nothing here redacts, and the language rules are entirely about who may SPEAK. A client may never choose LANG_UNIVERSAL: it is understood by everyone, so asking for it is asking to be understood by the other faction, and upstream logs it as a hacking attempt rather than a typo. A language with no skill (the binary ones, zombie) is not the same as an invented language id, which also has no skill — collapsing the two lets a client speak in language 9999. EARSHOT IS BY DISTANCE, NOT BY THE WATCHER SET: a yell carries 300 yards, far past visibility, so reusing the speaker's watchers makes a yell reach exactly as far as a say (40). The speaker is included — everyone's own line comes back from the server rather than being echoed by the client. A whisper echoes as CHAT_MSG_WHISPER_INFORM addressed to the RECEIVER; sending back a copy of the original shows the sender whispering to themselves. Message validation refuses rather than escapes: the line is cut at the first newline (and refused if it starts with one), control characters other than tab are refused, and any '|0' is refused because it closes a hyperlink body and a crafted link makes the receiving client act on an item or quest the sender chose. The length prefix on the wire counts BYTES and includes the terminator. LIMITS: whisper reaches only the same map — finding a player anywhere means touching them from this map's worker, which the tick model forbids (PLAN.md 4.2), and crossing it needs a queue into the other map's loop rather than a lookup. Guild, party, raid and channel lines are refused by omission, since none of those systems exist and accepting one silently would look delivered to the sender.

items.text: .commands framework — dispatch, security, and a starter set
items.note: Commands arrive as CMSG_MESSAGECHAT and are intercepted before the line is spoken — and BEFORE the alive check, since being dead is a thing you often want a command to fix and .revive typed by a corpse must not be swallowed as speech from someone who cannot speak. Replies go back as CHAT_MSG_SYSTEM to the sender alone, not as chat: nobody nearby sees a GM's .additem. The parser's rejections are the interesting part and they are all about NOT eating speech: a bare '.' or '!', a doubled prefix ('...' and '!!' are ordinary punctuation), and a prefix followed by a space. Swallowing those makes chat lose messages for reasons nobody can see, and the failure is invisible to whoever wrote the framework because they only type real commands. The line splits ONCE — name up to the first space, everything after is the argument string — or a command taking a name with a space in it is impossible to write. Security is declared on the command and enforced by the dispatcher, so a new command cannot forget to check; a test sweeps the table and fails if anything that changes state ships at player level. A command above your level reports as NOT EXISTING, the same answer as an unknown one — naming it is an invitation. Starter set: .help and .gps at player level; .additem, .learn, .setskill, .money, .level, .die and .revive above. .gps is the useful one — grid, cell, area, zone and the floor height under your feet, which is otherwise only visible through a debugger. .money is clamped at both ends: money is unsigned, so subtracting past zero wraps to ~42,000 gold.

phases.title: The tick
phases.summary: The threading model PLAN §4.2 calls the single most important constraint in the port.

items.text: Outbound packets go through a Channel with one writer task
items.note: Sending never touches a socket, so gameplay code on a map worker cannot block behind a slow client.

items.text: Header encryption begins at a POSITION IN THE SEND QUEUE, not a moment in time
items.note: Otherwise the plaintext challenge would be encrypted if the writer had not caught up.

items.text: Map is synchronous and lock-free; safety comes from the tick's ordering, not a mutex
World loop: drain the scheduler → drain sessions → run maps, in that order and never overlapping
MapUpdater — dedicated threads, not the thread pool, so a callback storm cannot starve a tick
One inbound queue per session, drained by whichever loop may run the packet at its front
items.note: The two-queue design in PLAN §4.2 was withdrawn: the M3 gate caught a character saving at its pre-movement position because logout overtook movement. Upstream's head-of-line blocking is what makes it correct.

items.text: Handlers resume on the loop that started them
items.note: ConfigureAwait(true) under the tick's SynchronizationContext, so a database answer never lands on a pool thread holding a Player.

items.text: Per-viewer update batching — one SMSG_UPDATE_OBJECT per tick instead of one per object
items.note: Logging in at Northshire went from 131 packets to 1.

items.text: Analyzer banning bare Task.Run in gameplay code
items.note: Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.BannedApiAnalyzers with src/BannedSymbols.txt, scoped to src/ via src/Directory.Build.props — tests may still use it. Bans every Task.Run overload plus Task.Wait and Task<T>.Result. RS0030 under TreatWarningsAsErrors, so it is a build failure, and src/ has no violations today.

items.text: AssertOwnerThread is not called anywhere yet
items.note: The invariant is documented and structural, but nothing fails loudly if a future caller breaks it.

items.text: Map workers default to 0 (inline). The pool is written and tested but unproven under load.
Creature updates are gated on cells near a player, as upstream does
items.note: The map used to update every creature it had ever loaded, every tick — so the cost of a tick followed where players had been, not where they were, and a map kept paying after everyone logged out. Measured across the same three harness runs: 50 slow ticks before, 2 after. The worst before was 3078 ms with ZERO sessions connected, purely ticking ~1,600 creatures nobody was near, each running an aggro range scan. Combat and respawn are deliberately exempt from the gate. Map.ActiveCreatureCount reports ticked against loaded.

items.text: The login tick is still over budget: ~161 ms, split between the deferred-work drain (~52 ms of database continuations resuming) and the map pass (~109 ms)
items.note: Corrected by measurement. The old note here blamed grid loading and said upstream splits the load per cell — both wrong. MapGridManager::LoadGrid calls LoadAllCellsInGrid(), so AzerothCore loads whole grids exactly as we do, and a grid load costs 0.8-1.8 ms for 133-687 creatures. The 31 ms first load was JIT warm-up. What remains is a one-off login cost, not a steady-state one: ~20 ms building the per-map spawn index (movable to startup, as upstream precomputes it) and the first grid load paying JIT.
